sections.h2: Where is the Montgomery County Recorder's Office in Dayton?
sections.html:
The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building, 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. Per the county's Recorder FAQ, the full deed and index collection, 1805 to the present, is kept there on books and microfilm.

Older material sits at the County Records Center and Archives, 117 South Main Street, 6th floor, reached by the Main Street elevator, at 937-225-6366. The office records, scans and indexes paperwork on the day it arrives, whether it comes by mail, over the counter or from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department. Documents go back in the mail the next business day, and the office works from 8 am to 4 pm on weekdays.

The Recorder is one of Ohio's oldest county offices. Ohio's General Assembly made it a required county office in 1803, the year Montgomery County was founded. Judges appointed the first recorders, and voters began electing them in 1829. Today the term is four years.

sections.h2: What does recording a deed cost in Montgomery County?
sections.html:
The county's own pages show two figures, so confirm the current one with the office before you bring a check. The Recorder FAQ quotes $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each added page. The eRecording page quotes $39.00 and $8.00.

Montgomery County recording charges as printed on two county Recorder pages
ChargeRecorder FAQeRecording page
First two pages$34.00$39.00
Each added page$8.00$8.00
Mortgage release or assignment, marginal notationNot listed$4.00
No clear 3-inch top margin on page one$20.00 standardization feeStandardization laws apply

The gap matches the statute. Section 317.32 sets $17 plus a $17 housing trust fund fee for two pages, which is $34, and lets a county add a preservation surcharge of up to $5. Pay at the counter in cash, or by check or money order made out to Montgomery County Recorder.

sections.h2: What must a Montgomery County deed contain?
sections.html:
The county lists the elements a clerk checks at the window. A deed needs:

  • The names of the buyers and sellers.
  • A legal description, which you can get from the Copy Center.
  • The sellers' signatures.
  • A preparation statement, if the deed was notarized in Ohio.
  • A Transfer or No Transfer stamp from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department, plus the Engineer's approval where the property calls for it.

Notarization follows the law of the state where the signer stood. The notary block has to show a statement, a signature and an expiration date. A mortgage adds the loan amount and the lender and borrower names.

Changing a name on a deed means a new deed, a stop at the Auditor for a stamp and then the Recorder. No new deed is generated when a loan is paid off. The lender records a Release or Satisfaction of Mortgage instead.

sections.h2: Which Montgomery County transfers must visit the Auditor first?
sections.html:
Anything that conveys land passes through the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department before recording. Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement, and the grantor pays the fee set in section 319.54, plus any transfer tax the county commissioners have levied.

The county's eRecording rules draw the line clearly. Mortgages, assignments and releases with no transfer can go in electronically through Simplifile. Deeds and anything needing a No Transfer stamp, such as a transfer on death designation, an easement or an affidavit that references a deed, must be mailed or walked through the Auditor's department first.

The Auditor and Engineer also publish conveyance standards, adopted August 2, 2021, governing legal descriptions and splits. Copies are on the Auditor's third and fifth floors and the Engineer's eighth floor at 451 West Third Street.

sections.h2: How do you find or print a Montgomery County deed?
sections.html:
Print any document you find on the Recorder's online search at no charge. If you cannot print, the Copy Center charges $2.00 per page, and certification adds $1.00. The office does not run title searches, but the 5th floor Public Research Area has public computers for doing your own.

  • Deeds, releases and liens are searchable by name on the county's online system.
  • To trace an older house, build the chain of owners from the grantee-grantor or tract index, then check the Auditor's tax lists for a jump in value that suggests new construction.
  • Veterans who recorded a DD214 can request a copy at no charge, and the Recorder issues a free Veteran ID card to those who record one.

Searching by street address happens on the Auditor's site instead of the Recorder's.

sections.h2: How do Montgomery County records help trace an older house?
sections.html:
The county's FAQ lays out a research route for anyone curious when a house was built. Start with the chain of ownership in the Recorder's deed records, using either the alphabetical grantee-grantor index or the tract index, which is organized by legal description. Both index types run from 1805 to the present, with deed books and microfilm for 1935 on and microfilm for 1805 through 1934.

  • At the Records Center and Archives, the alphabetical indexes cover 1805 to the present, and tract index microfilm covers 1805 to 1934.
  • The Auditor's tax lists run 1803 to 1954 as indexes and 1955 to 1985 as original books.
  • A jump of more than 50% in one year's taxable value usually points to construction or improvements.

The FAQ adds that taxable values were recorded at 35% of market value since 1973, and at 40 to 45% before that. The county says the research is the individual's job, though the archives answer questions at 937-225-6366. The Recorder's computerized tract index, one of few in-house systems of its kind, earned a National Association of Counties achievement award, and new records are indexed the day they arrive.

sections.h2: What is Montgomery County like for a house seller?
sections.html:
Dayton is the county seat, and the county spans 464 square miles in southwest Ohio, according to Wikipedia. It touches Miami, Clark, Greene, Warren, Butler, Preble and Darke counties. Besides Dayton, the cities include Kettering, Huber Heights, Centerville, Miamisburg, Vandalia, Trotwood and Englewood, and the villages are Farmersville, New Lebanon, Phillipsburg and Verona.

The county reports roughly 230,000 parcels. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts lists 539,598 residents in 2025 and 254,375 housing units. Owners occupy 62.5% of homes, the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $180,900, and median gross rent is $1,026. Median household income is $66,139.

Because more than a third of homes are rented, many sellers here are landlords. The Auditor's deed endorsement for residential rental property reminds the buyer to file landlord information under section 5323.02, so a rental sale carries one more form than an owner-occupied home.

faqs.q: What is the address of the Montgomery County Recorder?
faqs.a: The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building at 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. Records Center and Archives material is at 117 South Main Street, 6th floor.

faqs.q: How much does Montgomery County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: The Recorder FAQ prints $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 per added page, while the eRecording page prints $39.00 and $8.00. Call the office to confirm which figure applies the day you file.

faqs.q: Do I need the Auditor before the Recorder in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: Yes, for any deed. The Auditor's Deed Transfer Department stamps it Transfer or No Transfer and collects the conveyance fee, then the deed goes to the Recorder. Only non-transfer papers such as mortgages and releases can be e-recorded directly.

faqs.q: Is there a fee for a poorly formatted document in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder FAQ adds a $20 standardization fee when page one lacks a clear 3-inch top margin, and the eRecording page says all Ohio standardization laws apply.

faqs.q: Can I get a free copy of my Montgomery County deed?
faqs.a: Yes, if you print it yourself from the Recorder's online search. The Copy Center charges $2.00 per page if you cannot print, with certification costing $1.00 more.
